My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-sloping trajectory from a baseline near current market levels, which I anchored around the mid-350s for the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) or a similar broad index instrument. For the one-day horizon, I leaned heavily on recent price momentum and the tendency for markets to exhibit mean-reversion over very short windows, arriving at 356.5 as a near-status-quo estimate with only slight drift. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the figure slightly higher to 358.0, incorporating the mild positive drift that equities have historically exhibited on average while acknowledging that a single week is long enough for meaningful news flow to shift direction. The one-month estimate of 362.0 reflects a continuation of that modest upward drift, consistent with a low-volatility, no-recession baseline scenario where earnings and macro data come in roughly as expected.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon stretches, which reflects the well-established property that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility tends to be relatively contained barring surprise events, so the 346–367 range captures roughly one to two standard deviations of typical daily moves. By one week, the range widens to 338–378, incorporating the possibility of a meaningful macro surprise, a Fed communication shift, or geopolitical flare-up that could move markets several percent in either direction. At one month, the 320–405 range is deliberately wide because a month is long enough for a full repricing of risk sentiment, an earnings season surprise, or a significant change in interest rate expectations to materially alter the landscape.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals entirely. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in labor market data, a credit event in a systemically important institution, or an escalation in geopolitical conflict could trigger a flight-to-safety move that blows through the lower bounds. A sudden hawkish pivot from the Federal Reserve — perhaps driven by a CPI surprise — could similarly produce a sharp selloff. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong earnings season, a ceasefire in an active conflict zone, or a dovish Fed signal could send markets rallying well beyond the upper bounds of my intervals, particularly at the one-month horizon where cumulative positive surprises have more time to accumulate.

It is also worth acknowledging model uncertainty as a structural caveat.
